utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T, The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Crispian Smith for the Prosecution. We will be joined by Mr. Demirdjian after the first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We have -- you were about to say something, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think the same points about whether we could sit an extra session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was about to say that we have made the necessary inquiries, and bearing in mind Mr. Zecevic's difficulty as he articulated it yesterday, whereas we, of course, do not presume to say how any team divides up his work, we are surprised that the difficulty as expressed by Mr. Zecevic should present a great difficulty, probably being redundant, but -- Mr. Zecevic, the -- why -- all things considered and the support arrangement being in place, why should the Chamber having heard you nevertheless not grant the application to the extended sitting?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I just expressed my concerns. The concerns are that this is just the situation as it is. The witness -- the current witness is also my witness and his cross-examination has been postponed to this period of time and that was -- and the next witness is again mine, so I need to prepare both of them, but considering all the situation and the request of Ms. Korner and the reasons why she needs to leave on Tuesday, I believe that obviously there is no other way than to have an additional sitting this afternoon and we will make the arrangements necessary to deal with our witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I did speak to Mr. Zecevic and I'm very grateful to him for this. I wouldn't have had to ask had we not lost so much time on Monday. I worked up my cross-examination based on having a whole Monday to do it and because of the LiveNote and Mr. Krgovic's half an hour which turned into something rather more, but who am I to complain about that, Your Honours, I would be very grateful if we could sit just one extra session this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before we formally rule on that, Ms. Korner, there is a concern that the Chamber has which we think cannot be unexpressed, and we say had with the greatest respect to your experience as counsel and of course to the tactical or strategic methods that you employ in the conduct of your case, but it does seem to us that such time as is being used with this witness might be more efficiently used. Yesterday, for example, it appears to us that, an a inordinate amount of time was spent reformulating the same question with the -- to our mind, the predictable same answer from the witness and the -- we are inclined to -- I think the arrangements would be that we would sit from 2.30 to 3.45 this afternoon, but we would, with respect, ask you to bear in mind the concern that became apparent yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The other point of which I've just been reminded is that arithmetically you have 15 hours left which even with the extra session today it doesn't -- we don't see you finishing by -- we don't see this witness being finished by Monday, but it's something again for you to again bear in mind as we go forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, out of caution I asked for 20 hours. And out of caution based on -- not unexpectedly because most of the witnesses are like that, the witness is extremely lengthy answers and his attempt, we would suggest, to say the same thing over and over again. But I've taken on board what Your Honours say. If it has been my impression that my question has not been answered, and Your Honours think it has, well then obviously when one is on one's feet one doesn't get quite the same feel, but I take on board what Your Honours have said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So if there's nothing else, the usher would please escort the witness back on the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Bjelosevic. Before I invite Ms. Korner to continue her cross-examination, I should alert you in addition to reminding you you are still on your oath, I should alert you that you have over your several days here become used to the pattern of sitting of the -- of this trial, but with a view to completing your testimony, it has been decided that today there will be an extra sitting, so when the Court rises at the usual time of 1.45, it will not be for the day. We will return at 2.30 and then sit until 3.45. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, I want to just for a moment move away from the topics we were dealing with yesterday and ask you this: During the period from the outbreak of conflict around March/April until the end of June when the corridor was opened, you in Doboj still had access by road, didn't you, to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case I don't think I need to put up the map. Now, I want very briefly, please, to deal with the one document that yesterday we had a slight problem about and that's the full minutes of the 24th of March Assembly meeting which was held in Pale when Mico Stanisic was elected as minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have up, please, P439. It's tab 11 bis which was, I think, made clear last night [indiscernible] e-mail.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what I was putting to you was that the Doboj Municipal Assembly was set up, I think, two days later, came about as a result of effectively instructions -- Mr. Karadzic. Now, very briefly, did you ever come across or hear about the instructions commonly known now as Variant A and B, at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I only heard about that being mentioned, but I have never seen these documents, these instructions that you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you hear them being mentioned at the time, during the period, sometime between December 1991 and April 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I heard that later when certain processes started, Variant A and Variant B was being mentioned. I think it was after the year 2000, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask, however, that we have up on the screen in English page 16 and in the Bosnian version it is page 28.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I point out and I'll be corrected if I'm wrong, that this is the speech, the first speech made by Dr. Karadzic. And it's, in fact, the underlined paragraph in your language and it's the third paragraph in the English. Now, we know from the record of this that your cousin Milovan Bjelosevic was present at this Assembly meeting. Karadzic says: "I now ask you that following some instructions for national defence, information systems, et cetera, that will be given here, the real and sovereign authority of the Serbian Assembly and the Serbian people be established on the ground as soon as possible. As soon as we are informed that we have our own separate MUP, which will probably follow the coming session, all the newly-established municipalities should immediately set up police stations and all policemen should be withdrawn. Because that is, in fact, what life has taught us. Our policemen were forced out of the municipalities of Stari Grad," and I think from Visegrad as well, "policemen simply do not work together anymore and this fact must simply be accepted ..." Now, did you hear about this speech by Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Bjelosevic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What you read out just now what I see on the monitor, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But what he was saying that about establishing -- we have to have our own separate MUP and policemen simply do not work together anymore, was he expressing the same view that you have expressed throughout your evidence, namely that the different ethnicities could no longer work together?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, people fully worked together in Doboj and in some other stations. Truth to tell there was mistrust, but people did work together and how.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you didn't agree with --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said that this was the end of March, right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the 24th of March Assembly. The one when -- was the election of Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, it still functioned. There was polarisation, there was distrust, but the police stations in the area of CSB Doboj were still one, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we quickly please go to the next page both in English and B/C/S. And it's the paragraph -- no, sorry. That's not the next page in B/C/S. The next page should be -- it's page 13 in e-court. Page 30. That's not page 30, or shouldn't be. Yes, thank you very much. And in English, please, to -- yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we look -- if you look at the penultimate paragraph on that page in B/C/S, and we look, please, at the paragraph at the bottom that begins: "Newly-established municipalities must establish their organs as soon as possible, have their stamps made and start to work. The police, that is, our organs must be positioned at the border." Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, the witness doesn't have that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Isn't that the penultimate ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not that text.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. I thought it was. Yes, sorry, can we go to page 31. I hope that's it. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 30.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, no, forget that, it's a different number in the commuter system. Does that paragraph at the top say "newly-established municipalities"? I see Mr. Zecevic nodding. Do you see that, Mr. Bjelosevic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. As we saw a few days later, a couple of days later, I think, the Serbian municipality of Doboj was declared, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yesterday you showed it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And, yes, the final part I want to show you because it's going to lead into --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that is at page, I think it's 32 in English and it is at page 39 in B/C/S, I hope. No. No. English, please, is -- should be 00 -- no, 49. Four pages back please at the top, should be 02049 at the top. Thank you. Sorry, 2048, I am so sorry, back one more. And the B/C/S, I think that's the right --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does the paragraph there, second paragraph in B/C/S, and it's the middle paragraph in the English start, "You can be sure that numbers the police are quite sufficient." It must be "numbers of the police": "I know that the Serbs cannot do what the HOS is doing, to do things which are not based on law. We have a legal basis in the Law on Internal Affairs. And we have the insignia and at a desired moment, and this will be very soon, we can form whatever we want." I'm going to skip the next two sentences: "At the moment, all the Serbian municipalities, both the old ones and the newly-established one, would literally assume control of the entire territory of the municipality concerned. The Zvornik municipality takes control over everything that constitutes the Serbian municipality of Zvornik. At a given moment, in the next three or four day, there will be a single method used and you will able to apply it in the municipality you represent, including both things that must be down as well as how it to do them. How to separate the police force, take the resources that belong to the Serbian people and take command. The police must be under the control of the civilian authority, it must obey it, there's no discussion about it, that's the way it must be." Now, it took longer than the few days Mr. Karadzic spoke about Mr. Bjelosevic, but it's right, isn't it, in Doboj at the beginning of May, that's exactly what happened, the police and the army took control of Doboj town?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you would permit me, I would like to describe the situation. It happened in Doboj between the 2nd and the 3rd of May. But before that, in March, there was the take-over the public security station by the HOS and other paramilitary formations in Bosanski Brod. Then there was the take-over of the station in Derventa, then there was the situation in Odzak, and in some areas, some sort of camps had already been established where civilians were detained. The same thing happened in the Modrica municipality. So we were facing the situation which for us meant occupation of territory. Camps had already been set up, population had already been expelled from certain areas, civilian population, and it was only after all of this that the decision was made that at least Doboj should be saved from that, that the same thing should not happen in Doboj. There were forces that had been trained, equipped, and armed and that were ready to do the same thing in Doboj and that's when this decision was made by the command that Doboj should be taken over, in the military sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm reluctant to repeat the question, but you agree that's what happened, that the police and the army took over Doboj on the 2nd/3rd of May?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that it happened, and that it did happen pursuant to the decision of the military command. I also described the circumstances and the situation. All information pointed to the fact that it was only a difference of a few hours as to who was going to do it first.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, and where did that information come from?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a number of intelligence informations dating back from 1991 to that moment. They were becoming more and more frequent. And in April 1992, there was lots of activity of the Patriotic League, Green Berets and other forces that were concentrated around Doboj and that already held parts of some settlements. They were preparing the attack there. You also saw that some military inspectors came there to perform training. I've shown you the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, right. So your answer is this had nothing to do with any instruction or plan conceived by Mr. Karadzic and others as to the creation of the Serbian state?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we talk about the Serbian municipality of Doboj, I am not saying that it has nothing to do with it, but if we talk about what happened between the 2nd and the 3rd of May, I think that it has nothing to do with it. I really don't think that the commander would yield to some sort of political decisions and positions at that level because the commander was an officer, high-ranking JNA officer, a colonel at the time. And as I told you, it was really only a matter of time. It was really only a matter of who was going to do it first.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I hear what you say about that. Was that Colonel Stankovic you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's Cazim Hadzic. Stankovic was a major at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So when did he become a colonel?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether he ever became a colonel. If he did, maybe 1994 or 1995. I wouldn't know. He remained -- and I think that he remained a major. Stankovic was a major at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before the take-over, did you and Major Stankovic have meetings in your office?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed Major Stankovic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: I met Major Stankovic on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was that in order to discuss how to take over the town most efficiently?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't that kind of conversation. We talked about the general situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you aware that three days before the take-over of Doboj, Prijedor had been taken over in more or less the same manner, on the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the details about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Or Sanski Most shortly after the take-over of Doboj, did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we had a problem after the 3rd of May. We had a problem with the electricity and with the media, the function of the media, so during a certain period of time, I didn't know what was going on. The radio, the local radio did not work for a period of time. It was on or off, and I really didn't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can leave that document now. Can I just take you through the final documents that deal with the setting up of the Serbian MUP which you weren't asked about before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, at P353, tab 12A.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a telegram from Mr. Mandic dated the 31st of 1992 sent to all CSB heads and talking about the session on the 27th of March, the constitution had been proclaimed, the laws were adopted on internal affairs and then, setting out at the bottom of that first paragraph, what are going to be the Security Services Centre: Banja Luka, Trebinje, Doboj, Sarajevo, and at that stage Ugljevik. Did you get that telegram from Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what he says further on is that: "The Ministry of the Interior shall establish Security Services Centres at subordinate units. On the day when this law enters into force, the MUP Security Service Centres and public stations. Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next page please, in English. I think we need to go down the page a bit in the B/C/S version. We've now got two English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "... shall cease work on the territory of the Serbian Republic, while their jurisdiction and the duties of Internal Affairs organs shall be assumed by the organisational units of the MUP of the Serbian Republic of the BH. On the day that this law enters into force," et cetera et cetera, and then finally, "inform all employees of the SRBH MUP, with the content of the dispatch in a prompt and objective manner in order to avoid disruptive and undesirable situations." Now, did you understand that, Mr. Bjelosevic, to say that was effectively the end of the joint MUP? There was now a separate MUP for the Serbian Republic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How did you understand that then? Let's take the actual words. How did you understand the words, on the day when this law enters into force, the MUP security centres and public security stations of the socialist republic shall cease work on the territory of the Serbian Republic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't understand me when I said that I didn't understand it that way. Of course, I read what it says here and it's quite clear what it says here, but you should try to understand the situation in which the Doboj CSB and I, as its chief, found ourselves. You should try to understand the general situation. I had to think with my own head at the time. I had to figure out what it meant, and I also had to figure out what exactly was the situation that we were facing. As you had a chance to see, throughout April we functioned as part of the MUP of the Socialist Republic of BiH and we used the communications as long as they functioned. So when I said that that was not my understanding, I didn't think that that was something realistic and that it was something that should have been done at the time. Our management structure was, well, what it was, and in the centre itself it functioned quite well. It is true that in the field the situation was rather complex and difficult, especially when it comes to Bosanski Brod and Odzak. Brod had been separated by then, and we were trying to do everything we could in order to keep the system of security stable.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's two different things. I'm not asking you what you did, and I accept what you did. I asked whether it was clear to you that that was the end of a joint MUP, that there were to be two separate MUPs from what Mr. Mandic's telegram said? Not what you did, we'll come on to what you did.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite clear what it says here, but I also have to tell you that after this dispatch, there was a series of dispatches. Yes, it was agreed and there was a collegium with the minister, Mr. Delimustafic, then there was denial that it didn't take place. So the situation was quite -- quite confusing. So at that moment it wasn't really possible to come to the clear conclusion that that was the end of it. Something was going on, something was possible, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Believe you me, Mr. Bjelosevic, I'm not going to ignore what then happened. You will go through those documents very clearly. But that instruction on its face, can we just -- could you just answer this yes or no, clearly was the signal and was the end of a joint MUP if that instruction was followed? That's all I've asked.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if you look at this document in isolation, then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, before you got the telegram sometime between the meeting in February in Banja Luka and this telegram from Mr. Mandic, had you attended a meeting in Sarajevo with other senior members of the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In which you had attended with other members of the MUP from Doboj? Anything like that ever happen? Any kind of meeting in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think the witness just answered no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I said -- but I'm changing slightly, the question was other senior members of the MUP, so I'm asking any kind of meeting in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During February and March, if I remember that well, I think that I did go to Sarajevo to the headquarters of the MUP. That was the Borisa Kovacevica at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And who did you see there, did you see Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Or Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that I met Mr. Mandic because we had a number of problems related to crime in the area of the Doboj centre, so I often communicated with him related to this issue. And also with Amir Mladic, he was the chief of the narcotics bureau. I think that that was his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So did you attend -- sorry, when you saw Mr. Mandic, were there other senior members of the Serbian joint MUP, Socialist Republic MUP, present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to remember the names, but certainly somebody was there. And if I'm not mistaken, I think that there was Dazdarevic, I don't remember his first name. He was the chief of the crime prevention administration while Momcilo Mandic was assistant minister, so the two of them communicated often. I also used to go to the police department at the same time and I talked to some of the inspectors and the chief there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Zupljanin there at any meeting in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean us together in the MUP, I can't remember anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because there's no mystery to all of this, Mr. Bjelosevic. Mr. Zupljanin, when he spoke at the meeting in Belgrade in July, which you went to and which you have got notes, says it seems a long time since we met in Sarajevo. So can you give us an idea of when you had a meeting in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that we met in Sarajevo under such circumstances. I really don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have up, please, on the screen, the document which is 20002. Seems somewhat improbable, but it's tab 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, same day as Mr. Mandic's telegram: "We hereby inform you that a meeting will be held at 1100 hours on the 1st of April at Doboj CSB at which the current security situation and upcoming tasks will be discussed." I take it, Mr. Bjelosevic, that that meeting was as a direct result of Mr. Mandic's order that all employees should be informed of the contents of his dispatch; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This has absolutely nothing to do with that dispatch. This is a working meeting of the police station commanders convened by Vojo Blagojevic who was chief of the police in the centre. So it was something that had nothing to do with it. Something quite separate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You were asking the SJB chiefs or the SJB to the SJBs for all those places to come to a meeting, and it was a sheer coincidence that it was the same day that the new Law of Internal Affairs was coming into effect and Mr. Mandic had ordered you to tell everybody about it. Sheer coincidence, is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, I believe the witness said that -- gave the name of the person who convened the meeting. And, Ms. Korner, on page 17/3, you were asking -- if we can have the base on that, for that question. She said to the witness, you were asking the SJB chiefs to come to a meeting, and the witness explained who convened the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, if the meeting had nothing to do, Mr. Bjelosevic, with anything that was happening as a result of Mr. Mandic's telegram and this was a standard meeting that Mr. -- Mr. -- what you said his name was -- the gentleman who signed on your behalf, why did it go out under your name?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when something was sent on behalf of the CSB, the name of the chief of the centre had to be written at the bottom, as a rule. But also chief departments in accordance with their own lines of work, in this particular case we are dealing with line 01, police, they also worked and held meetings with their subordinates in their hierarchy. This has to do with Vojo Blagojevic, chief of police in that period, and he is inviting the commanders of police stations to a working meeting. If I was the one inviting them, it isn't logical that I would be inviting the station chiefs. So it wasn't me. It was the chief of the police department who did that in accordance with the line of work of the police. He invited them to a working meeting and this is something quite ordinary. Now, the fact that there is a coincidence about the date, you have to believe me that it had really absolutely nothing to do with that. You can be absolutely certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Bjelosevic. Did you ever hold a meeting at the CSB with the personnel from the SJBs under the Doboj CSB to tell them what was happening about Mr. Mandic's telegram?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never held such a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it would be totally wrong to suggest to you that you did hold such a meeting, you told the police officers that there was going to be this divided MUP and that the CSB Doboj would now be under the Serbian Republic, that the non-Serb police walked out, and, thereafter, the police were divided on ethnic lines in Doboj. Nothing like that ever happened?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That kind of meeting with that kind of agenda, that kind of topic, no, I never held a meeting like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's just move, then, if we may speedily through the remainder of the documents that dealt with this period.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Have a look, please, next at tab 14 which is ... Sorry, Your Honours, I've just lost my note for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, Your Honours, perhaps it needs to be clarified 17, 24, 25, it is recorded as: "If I was the one inviting them, it isn't logical that I would be inviting the station chiefs." I believe the witness said something else. Perhaps this can be clarified with the witness for the purposes of clear record, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bjelosevic, can you just tell us again what you said about --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was explaining what it was about. The police chief in accordance with his line of work invited --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone off, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Invited the commanders of police station. And I said if I was the one sending out the invitation, it would be logical. So I didn't sign the dispatch and I didn't invite anybody. It was Vojo Blagojevic who invited the commanders. That's what I wanted to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the interpreters didn't hear the part of the witness's answer, so if I can kindly ask the witness to speak slowly into the microphone and then we have a clear answer because we are losing time like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we ask -- Mr. Bjelosevic, can you just repeat your answer but please, please, please, try and keep your answers short.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to be as brief as possible. I was explaining the dispatch which you claimed had do with Momcilo Mandic's dispatch, and my point was that the two didn't have anything to do one with another. So I explained who the signature belonged to that we can see in the dispatch that was sent to -- from the CSB Doboj out into the field. I said that it was Mr. Vojo Blagojevic who signed the dispatch. He was chief of the police department in the CSB Doboj at the time. As can be seen in the dispatch, he invited commanders of police stations within the area of the CSB Doboj to attend the meeting and I made a comparison. I said, had I been the one inviting them, would it not have been logical that I would have invited chiefs of stations, but this isn't my signature nor are the chiefs of stations invited, rather, it was the way I explained it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you happy now, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, I would be interested to know if you attended the meeting which had been called by Mr. Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so. It was within their line of work and that was the nature of the meeting. That was why he called the commanders so it was only one part of the service that was supposed to meet and it was standard practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Were you informed of the agenda of Mr. Blagojevic's meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see it in the dispatch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, just to make it absolutely clear, when you said he invited chief of police, the chiefs of police, that is chief of police as opposed to chiefs of station; is that right? That's how I understand the transcript, that you make a difference between chiefs of police and they were the persons Mr., whatever his name is, Blagojevic, invited, and you said would I have invited people, then I would have invited the chief of station, the chiefs of station; is that correct in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously wishing to be as clear as possible, I quite unfortunately inserted this hypothesis about me and the chiefs of stations, and I have this feeling that I should perhaps give you the structure again and how it worked. There were public security stations within the area which had their chiefs, and these chiefs were directly subordinated to the chiefs of centres. So, my aside was an unfortunate one. In terms of the line of the work the police stations, which were part of public security stations, were uniformed police. At the time it was called milicija, and Mr. Blagojevic was their direct superior and would invite them to working meetings which had to do with their line of work, i.e., the line of work of uniformed police. And this is what the meeting had to do with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Could we have up on the screen, please, document 1D00136, tab 12B.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is actually the radio version of -- it was apparently sent to Radio Sarajevo on the same day, 31st of March, but also sent to the CSB chief and it's the response by Mr. Delimustafic to Mr. Mandic's telegram. Did you get that as well?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did receive it. As I'm reading it, I think it is one of the dispatches I referred to as having arrived one after another.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, wasn't it shown to you by Mr. Zecevic when he showed you all the documents?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I'm reading it through to be sure of what I'm telling you. Yes, we did receive the dispatch, whether it was on the same day or on the following day, but they arrived one after another.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Urging everybody to ignore Mr. Mandic's attempt, as it was put, to divide the MUP, do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as you pointed out when you were giving evidence to Mr. Zecevic, for the next month until the 2nd/3rd of May, you did in fact report, didn't you, to both MUPs, the socialist republic and also to the RS? That's right, isn't it, Mr. Bjelosevic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either not everything was interpreted to me or what was it that I didn't put into the report that I sent to the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Serbian Republic?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question. No, I won't. I'll ask the same question again very slowly. During the next month, that is of April, until the take-over on the 2nd/3rd of May, you as chief of the Doboj CSB reported to both the old BiH MUP, headed by Alija Delimustafic, and the Serbian Republic MUP, headed by Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now the question is clear. Thank you. Until the end of April, reports were sent to the Ministry of the SRBiH. If I remember correctly, in the second half of April, two reports were sent -- or, rather, after the 16th of April, after the events in Derventa and at Cardak, a report was also sent to the Ministry of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. The answer to my question is yes; is that right? You did report both to BiH MUP, the old one, and to the RS?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after the 16th of April, after the events at Cardak, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was at that period that according to you, you stopped taking notes in your notebook of whom you met, the meetings you attended; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know whether this expression translates into Serbian, I'll try to find out, but do you know an expression such as someone who tries to run with the hare and hunt with the hounds? I don't know if it translates at all into the Serbian language. In other words, that a man cannot serve two masters? Is that an expression you are familiar with, Mr. Bjelosevic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That you can't serve two masters; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, allow me to express my dissatisfaction with the way the honourable Prosecutor is treating me. On Monday, although in a somewhat embellished form, she said that I was lying. If you translate what she said, it means that I was lying, and what Mr. Stanisic and I were doing at the time was just a screen, it was just a front that we were window dressing and suppressing things. Yesterday, she was undermining my intelligence, and I think that that is quite irrelevant as to whether the witness is intelligent or not for his evidence. So I would like my dignity to be respected here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, please rest assured that it is a part of the duty of the Trial Chamber to ensure that witnesses are treated fairly. But in terms of these proceedings, it is the duty of counsel without, to use your words, disrespecting the intelligence of a witness, to probe and test a witness's evidence, particularly in cross-examination, and that is all that Ms. Korner is doing. If she crosses over the line, the Chamber would remind her of that, but so far I haven't heard anything which is offensive and which you -- which is an improper question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, what you were trying to do for that first month was to serve two masters, I suggest to you, because you weren't sure at that stage what was going to happen, which was going to be the right side?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that. In that period of time, I invested to all my efforts to maintain the situation stable and to preserve peace, and you can call it whatever you like. I had by that time occasion to see what happened in the areas caught by war. I saw what happened to the victims and refugees and all the evil that comes with the war, and I wanted to preserve a state of peace.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, Mr. Bjelosevic, how could you possibly remain with one foot in the old MUP and one foot in a MUP which on your own assessment from Mr. Mandic's telegram and from what happened thereafter was a totally separate police organisation?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case, allow me to give you a broader answer to that. In some of your questions you seem to be proceeding from a view that at the time Bosnia-Herzegovina was an isolated and independent state, and that somebody tried to forcibly separate from that state. This wasn't true. Yugoslavia was still in place at the time. There had been hostilities in Croatia by that time, and it was already obvious what war meant. Pragmatic solutions were sought to preserve peace. At the time Bosnia-Herzegovina was politically divided. At that time in April, Bosnia-Herzegovina did not have all of its legitimate representatives starting from the Presidency to the Assembly to the government. All of these were already divided. Try and picture yourself in such a situation where you are in charge of a service under those circumstances surrounded by a large presence of the military, paramilitary, and, if you will, rogue groups, et cetera. I don't see that there is anything bad in the practice of informing both parts of what were the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. To me, they were legitimate and legal. Both Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and Mr. Koljevic, as well as Madam Biljana Plavsic, Mr. Boras and all the members of the Presidency, all the deputies who were lawfully elected in 1990, all of them were, to my mind, lawful representatives. I'm telling you this to understand my position. When you say that I'm keeping my feet in different positions, let me tell you that I didn't want to side with politics in 1997 and the same applied to 1992. I don't know if you now understand my position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Just one final question and then it's time for the break. In your mind, is this what you are saying, the declaration of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the constitution of the Serbian Republic, the passing of the Law of Internal Affairs, that had absolutely no effect on legitimacy of the Bosnian -- the old Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the legitimacy of the old Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as you put it. I'm talking about the legitimacy of the Presidency members, the legitimacy of the Assembly men, the deputies, and the legitimacy of the ministers who were members of the government and who subsequently were divided. The legitimacy conferred upon them by the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina had not been taken away from them in the meantime. That's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, you can it's time for the break. I'm not going to pursue this any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, one follow-up question: So you were reporting to both MUPs, let's say, during the second half of April, and then at the end of April or at the beginning of May, you stopped reporting to the Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP. What triggered that decision in your mind? There must have been something that made you decide not to report anymore to the Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP. What was it that made you take that decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What happens was that all the links and communications were severed, and between the end of April, up until the period when the communications were up and running, no reports were sent out, and then in early May --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: In late May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The centre basically closed down, as I said. And then it was practically non-existent until sometime in July when it was reinstated. So there was a period of some two months or two and a half months when the centre was non-existent and when no reports were sent out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So then what you are saying then is that the decision not to send reports to the Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP has been taken in July when things started working again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't a decision on my part to discontinue communications, it was force majeure. And the same went for the CSB and its closing down. The fact of the matter was that we didn't have a territory to speak of, we didn't have the personnel, and the centre, as such, didn't exist. You didn't have the police department or the crime police, personnel service, law affairs. In other words, the centre, as such, wasn't there. It didn't function. Later on when the communications system was restored as you said in July, everyone established their own communication system in their respective areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Are you saying now that the fact that you stopped reporting to the Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP and only reported to the Serbian MUP anymore, to the Republic of Serbia MUP was only something that had to do with communication lines? Are you saying that if you would have had communication lines with the Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP, you would have continued to report to them, even in July and afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what would have happened. It's a hypothesis. But I know what happened and that's what I'm describing. The communications system was non-existent. Every side had by that time taken up their respective areas militarily. And as for the centre itself, I think I've already explained in detail how the matters stood, and if need be I can repeat. It was the state of affairs as it existed in the field, as it developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, again there is -- I can see that there is confusion, but that is because a part of his answer was not recorded and it's not in the -- it's not in the record, in transcript. And it obviously was not translated to you. Perhaps after the break I can explain what it is before the witness is brought in and then you can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- verify that with the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the break and resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, this morning when we were speaking about the time that was used by the OTP, there was a little error in the calculations. It seems to be something more than seven hours, rather than five but you realise that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honours. In any event, not just for the reasons that I've expressed, I would be concluding my cross-examination well within the 20 hours, of course subject to what I put answering the questions shortly. But, Your Honours, I know Mr. Zecevic wants to address you before he comes in on what was or was not said, but there is one point that I should have dealt with earlier this morning. When Your Honour Judge Delvoie yesterday asked me about exhibiting documents, of course I just had the intercepts in mind, which I didn't intend, but I forgot I also put to him his diary entry and I would like, obviously, to exhibit that. It's the diary entry for the 10th of February. 65 ter 20103.01.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit P02323.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am wondering if -- because Ms. Korner showed to the witness also the entry on the 11th of February.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Mr. Krgovic did, but I'm perfectly happy for that also to be exhibited as well. I see, the 10th and the 11th run together, it's one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's why I was just making sure that it's one document, yes. Thank you. May I, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before the break His Honour Judge Delvoie was posing a couple of questions to the witness. However, the witness answered that due to the severance of the communication lines between the -- at the end of April or beginning of May, he wasn't sending any reports either to BiH MUP, the SR BiH MUP or MUP of Republika Srpska, so no reports to either of the MUPs were sent, and that part wasn't recorded in the transcript. I don't know if it was translated because I didn't have my earphones on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it isn't explicitly in the transcript, but that's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm sorry, I just wanted to be of assistance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, on the documents again, this morning you showed the document under tab number 12. Do I take it you don't tender it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I do tender it. Your Honours, for some reason I thought this has always been an exhibit but hasn't, and I would like to have that made an exhibit as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I correctly remember, this is the 1st of April, the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think I offered it as exhibit and actually was asked by the Trial Chamber what is the relevance and then Ms. Korner said that she is not objected and I think it was admitted, but I have to check. I think it was admitted as Defence document already during the direct examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I thought so too but if we are both --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: During the direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Under 65 ter number 2002?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I don't think so. I think we uploaded the document as our -- but I will have to check, Your Honours, and come back to you about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, while we are waiting we'll just check. Mr. Smith thinks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we can have the witness back in now, can we?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was exhibited as 1D455 and I do remember I said, for the reasons that we can all see, that I didn't object. Had Your Honour finished asking questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, just came up on the screen before but just let's confirm, please, which is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could I have up, please, Exhibit P1410, tab 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, that's your appointment, isn't it, as the -- for the moment temporary chief of CSB Doboj in the Ministry of the Internal Affairs of the Serbian Republic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you -- did you get a copy of that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can see at the top of the page that it was sent on the 19th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was it at that stage that you decided that you would go with the RS MUP?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I already answered that question but I'll repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, all right. Don't, please. During the course of April, did you set up police stations in, first of all, a place called Kalenderovci in the Derventa municipality?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The war time schedule envisaged a war police station there, and at that place they assembled both the war police and the personnel that had left the police station in Derventa. That's when they joined this station that had been envisaged by the war organisational chart.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Whether it was envisaged or not, was it you who were responsible for the establishment of that war police station?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I hope Your Honours won't think that I'm unnecessarily repeating the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to underline that this had been envisaged by the war time organisational chart and that particular police station had been mobilised and fully functioning. And during the events that took place in and around Derventa, the personnel from the public security station in Derventa joined that station and the station goals in Osinja. They are all the stations envisaged by the plan and they existed. They had the personnel. Everything had already been set up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you issue the necessary orders and instructions for the establishment of this police station envisaged by a war plan?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That had been done much earlier, before I was appointed the chief of the CSB in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did that police station start operating in April?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was even before. When all the war police station were mobilised, when the reserve forces were mobilised, that's when that station began working.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that station entirely staffed by Serb members of the MUP or reserve MUP?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is one of many stations and it's difficult for me to remember that now. But if I'm not mistaken whether it was Mehmedovic or Subasic I remember that there was a Muslim in the reserve police. I remember that because of the name. And as for the rest of the personnel, I really don't know. It was just one of the many reserve police stations in the territory of the Doboj CSB.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you also in April form or put into operation a police station at a place called Osinja also in the Derventa municipality?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not form that one. It had also been envisaged by the previously-established plan about the organisation and systemisation of the reserve police stations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: During April, was that police station brought into full operation by you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had become operative even before, as far as I can remember, when all other stations became operative. And I have to underline that the order about the mobilisation of the reserve police stations was issued by the MUP of the RS BiH -- SR BiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that, the Socialist Republic as opposed to the Serb Republic. In April, was that police station entirely manned by Serb members of the MUP or reserve MUP?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know but because Osinja and the neighbouring villages are inhabited only by Serbs, I assume that probably the manpower was also of Serb ethnicity. That's my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I won't go over with you a few matters concerning the Law on Internal Affairs. Before we do that, when you were giving evidence in response to questions by Mr. Zecevic, you were shown a document which is the Defence document tab 36. I'll give you a number in a minute, but you can turn it up if you've still got your bundle. It had the number, I think, 1D004779. I think it's now an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you say tab 36?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I did. It's document 8th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's 1D257. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you told Mr. Zecevic at page 19549 that you were familiar with this dispatch, it comes from the department from defence preparations: "Another flagrant example of the violation of the basic laws and regulations governing Internal Affairs ... inconceivable and incompatible with all rules and regulations in force at the time that Territorial Defence units should be subordinated to the police stations contrary to all republican and federal regulations." Now, do I take it from that that you are familiar with republican and federal regulation, Mr. Bjelosevic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I would like you, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Or I would like to have up on the screen, it's the document at tab 1A and it's L0026. It's part of the law library, Your Honours. I'll find my own copy of it. We have Article -- Your Honours, I'm so sorry, I keep doing this. We moved the document at the break and now I can't find it again. Yes. It's page 12 in English and page 16 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this deals -- these articles of the law on -- law on something. All People's Defence. Thank you. Dealing with the Territorial Defence. Article 105 says it's the widest form of organised All People's armed Defence. Article 106 describes what the Territorial Defence is about. And then Article 107, please, is that the whole page, probably is. All right: "The Presidency of the Socialist Republic pursuant to a decision of the Presidency of the SFRY under Article 5 of the federal law, shall order the use of the Territorial Defence units to carry out tasks of public peace and order and to carry out other tasks of social self-protection." Next part: "The Territorial Defence units shall be subordinated to the interior affairs organ in charge whilst performing duties and tasks from Article 105.1 of the federal law." Were you familiar with that provision, Mr. Bjelosevic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 105 of the federal law is referenced here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we are looking at the republican law.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Appreciating that there are all sorts of preconditions and there are other laws involved, I'm asking you in the light of your assertions to Mr. Zecevic the other day, that this was a completely and utterly illegal order, whether you were familiar with the provisions of this law that in certain circumstances the Territorial Defence could be subordinated to the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But we should take a look here about the particular circumstances, what exactly is stipulated by Article 105. That's one thing. And the other thing, here we see that the Presidency of the SR BiH is mentioned, the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, pursuant to a decision of the Presidency of the SFRY, et cetera, and here we have an order that was not issued by the Presidency of the SR BiH. If you find that particular dispatch, you will see that it wasn't the order issued by the Presidency but that it was a decision made by the government.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bjelosevic, all that I'm asking you at this moment is whether you were familiar with this provision, leaving aside its bringing into effect in this day, did you know about this provision?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know about this provision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you don't know, do you, whether this particular dispatch being signed by Mr. Pusina, I think it was, wasn't it? Sorry, I better get it out again. Yes. You don't know on the 8th of April from this dispatch whether or not the required steps had been gone through?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what kind of required steps you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Whatever steps were required to bring this legal -- this law into effect, you don't know whether or not when Mr. -- sorry, Mr. Jasarevic sent out this dispatch, whether or not the legal requirements had been complied with?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conditions stipulated by the law were not met. There was no order issued by the Presidency, and secondly, volunteers as a category -- and take a look at the dispatch at its last line, I mean, it's even more open here. It says here "volunteers or other military conscripts subordinated to the SJB," so anybody can walk in and say, Hello, I'm going to be a member of the police. This has absolutely no foundations and I definitely -- I still claim that this is unlawful. There are at least two reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All I'm concerned about is the assertion that you made: It is inconceivable and incompatible with all the rules and regulations in force at the time that Territorial Defence units should be subordinated to police stations. Would you agree that was an exaggerated statement in the light of this?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would have to take a look at the federal laws and make a connection between the federal and republican laws if we were to obtain a proper and correct answer to this question. What comprised the armed forces of Yugoslavia? At the top of the pyramid there was one unified command and that was the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I am going to stop you, Mr. Bjelosevic. I agree we've spent a long time talking about how these laws came into effect. All I'm asking you is whether you accept what you said earlier was an exaggerated statement of the position? If you don't accept that, you can simply say, No, I don't accept it.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree. I still claim that this is unlawful.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. That's all I was asking. Can we look, please, for a little bit at the Law on Internal Affairs that was passed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That will be, please, it's P530 and we put it in at tab 10A.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The law was actually passed on the 28th of February, published in the Gazette, as we can see, on the 23rd of March, 1992, and came into effect, I think it was seven days later. Yes, the 30th of March. Now, you were familiar with the old BiH law, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in most respects this law promulgated by the Serbian Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina was the same although there were some differences?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is quite similar, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in Article 5, the minister is in charge of Internal Affairs listed in Article 3 which are the tasks and activities related to public security, national security, and then identity cards and all the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have that article.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Korner, the question was: "In Article 5, the minister is in charge ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But the reading of the Article 5 says "the ministry," not "the minister."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I accept the correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you see that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. The minister of the interior was the head of the ministry; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The hierarchy of the Ministry of Internal Affairs was the minister, under that, if there was one, a deputy minister - there wasn't in this case - the assistant ministers, the chiefs of the CSBs and the heads of the SJB. That was the hierarchy, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, also the heads of department at headquarters. You omitted that. But that was it. Basically that is the structure involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the reporting system through the hierarchy was strictly enforced, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because that's one of the complaints that you made that your level of -- in the hierarchy as CSB chief was being ignored by chiefs of SJB stations, some of them who would report directly up to the ministry?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they came to the centre as they carried out that activity of theirs. We said what the stations these were and in what sense all of this happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that. But I mean, I'm just saying that as far as you were concerned chiefs of the public security stations, the SJBs, should report to you, and it was your job then to report up to the ministry itself?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but there are situations in accordance with this instruction about current and temporary reporting when a station can directly report. What I complained about had less to do with reporting. It had more to do with this bypassing as it were. The chief, a particular station, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If the minister issued an order which was then sent to a CSB chief via one of the heads of departments or assistant ministers, was that something that you were obliged to obey?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was binding, but if you see that something is unlawful then, as you could see, I reacted. I indicated that this was something that was unlawful.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely. But provided it was in the law, it was a binding order?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look, please, at Article 10, which is on the same page. It's the next page in English. 3

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which article?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Article 10. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can it please be enlarged?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll enlarged it for you. It says: "Public security stations shall assist in the execution of activities and tasks within the remit of other state organs or enterprises and other legal entities exercising public authority as prescribed by law, when physical resistance is encountered or can be reasonably expected in the course of these execution of these activities and tasks." The chief of the public security station shall decide on the form and extent: "If he expects that organised and large scale physical resistance will be encountered in extending the assistance described in paragraph 1 of this Article, or that weapons will be used, the chief of the public security station must obtain the consent of the minister of the interior (hereinafter, the minister) before reaching a decision as outlined in the previous -- preceding paragraph." So does that mean if there was a question, for example -- well, perhaps you can give us an example. What is meant here by other state organs or enterprises?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In police jargon this was called assistance, "asistencija." For example, other state organs are supposed to carry out a decision, say, of an inspectorate. Let me talk, say, about construction project. The construction inspectorate forbids the building of a particular edifice and then the inspectorate makes a decision stating that what has been built so far has to be destroyed, and the police offers its assistance in that way, allowing the construction inspectorate to tear down what had been built until then. That also happened when people were supposed to be moved out of certain premises. There are various situations of that kind. At the request of a particular organ, an assessment is made and as you saw in the third paragraph of this article, if it is assessed that this is very risky then even the consent of the minister is required, if weapons are to be used, for instance, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, let's take another example. If, for example, the Municipal Assembly of Doboj decided that no one should be allowed to carry fire-arms, and issued an order that they were to surrender all fire-arms and the persons ordered was apparent [indiscernible] to do that. And the police were brought in to execute a lawful order made by the Municipal Assembly, if force was to be used in those circumstances, would the consents of the minister have to be obtained?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether you have chosen a good example, even though it is hypothetical. Municipal Assemblies can pass decisions on public law and order referring to the work of the catering industry, for instance. But as for prohibiting the carrying of fire-arms, I'm not sure that the Municipal Assembly did have that kind of authority. If people had licences, then they were allowed to have weapons. They could have, for instance, forbidden people to enter the premises of the Assembly with fire-arms, if that's what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Leave aside the particular thing I just -- but if that was the situation, if the municipal body in charge had issued an instruction which had to be carried out by the police because it was a lawful instruction and there was going to be resistance and that was obvious to everybody, would the consent of the minister before force was used have to be obtained?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the sake of clarity, for each and every situation when the police provides assistance, an assessment is made. That is to say, the risk is assessed and also what could possibly happen when a decision is being enforced. If it is established as is clearly stated in paragraph 3 of Article 10 that there can be larger scale resistance and use of fire-arms, then it was necessary to obtain the concept of the minister for providing that kind of assistance, "asistencija."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's move then to specific matters dealt with on this topic about laws made by the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Article 27, please, which is on page 4 in English and page -- I think it's 4 also in B/C/S, Cyrillic:

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "In addition to the activities and tasks set out in the rules on the internal organisation of the ministry, a public security station shall implement regulations passed by the Municipal Assembly relating to law and order, road safety, as well as other regulations in the domain of Internal Affairs that have been passed by the Municipal Assembly." Going back to what Dr. Karadzic said in March, he said the police have to be under civilian authorities, and that's correct, isn't it, the police and the executive, they carry out the lawful regulations made by either the Assembly of the state or the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right when you say that they work in carrying out regulations passed by the Municipal Assembly in accordance with the Law on Internal Affairs in respect of those particular elements. However, as far as public security stations are concerned and their relationship with the Municipal Assemblies and the Executive Boards that existed at the time as the executive organs of the Municipal Assemblies, then there had to be information. The public security station had to function on a horizontal plane as we called it. They had to inform the Assembly about matters that had to do with that area. However, they did not have to submit reports that would have to be adopted ultimately. Also, in certain areas the Municipal Assembly did not have the right to issue any kind of orders, but what is stipulated here specifically, yes, that is indeed the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I absolutely agree. There were certain areas where orders had to be issued through the line of the chain of command and all that the Municipal Assembly could do was request information?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. And Article 28 merely sets out the CSBs and then Article 31 I think is what we are all thinking of -- sorry, which is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was enlarged and now you had it removed. Did you say 28?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, 31. I mentioned 28 in passing, Mr. Bjelosevic, but it's Article 31: "If so requested by the Municipal Assembly and its executive committee, a Security Services Centre and a public security station shall submit reports, information, and other data relating," I think the word must be missed out, "to the situation and problems in the area in which and for which they have been established." Article 32 on the same lines: "The Municipal Assembly and its executive committee may submit opinions to the ministry at its seat, initiate proposals," and so on. Now, when the Municipal Assembly could not meet because there was a state of emergency or an imminent threat of war and its functions were being carried out by a Crisis Staff, the Crisis Staff had the same abilities, didn't it, in respect of the police as had the Municipal Assembly subject to verification of its decisions at a later stage when the Assembly was able to meet.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you were reading that out, could you please give me that provision as well, the article.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, I'm putting a question to you whether you accept that the Crisis Staff legislation and discussions do not lie in the Ministry of Internal Affairs. I'm asking you -- sorry, in the Law on Intern Affairs. I'm asking you whether you accept that the powers exercised under the law by the Municipal Assembly when it couldn't meet and a Crisis Staff was in its place, it could also exercise those powers?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to be quite frank and say that as far as I'm concerned Crisis Staffs in that situation and at the time and in the form in which they existed were quite a grey zone because Crisis Staffs, as you could see from various documents, came into being as, say, the Crisis Staff of the Croat people, the Crisis Staff of the Serb people, the Crisis Staff of the Muslim people, and so on and so forth, and then later on, how should I put this, they were re-organised territorially. They were reformulated, as it were. As far as Crisis Staffs or this or that, people are concerned, then, at least as far as I know, and I'm not saying I know everything, I really have to be clear on that, they were not based on law and that is how they started organising themselves. And then, well, that's the way it was. But if you take into account the circumstances involved and I would dare say that it was the entire area of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was involved, the territory was disjointed, there was hardly any communication and there would then be some justification for Crisis Staffs because somebody had to take over the role of governing and organising life in these areas too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
