I heard that they arrived there in order to help the evacuation of the JNA units who were then being evacuated towards Serbia. And then when the territory was cut off and the road towards Serbia were closed, they remained. They organised training camps and what I know, if that's of any relevance here, is that that was training of highest quality. Everybody who underwent that training successfully received a red beret as proof that they had undergone this particular training successfully. So the people who were trained in such a way were then sent to JNA units, sometimes as squad commanders, sometimes in other status. Later, there were people who had undergone this training who joined the police. So according to what I know, the Bozovic's people were 10 or 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That's all I want to ask you about that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Last document I want to show you on this topic of the take-over, could we have a look, please at a video. It's under tab 16A, 202121, and there's a transcript. There is sound for this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Many of them after the furlough wished to continue their way. Every war has its heros. On this assignment, we met Joja, not the one from Mount Kozara, from the last war, but Joja from Krajina. "They call me Joja. I'm known at all front lines, and let's keep it that way. "What front lines have you been at? "Well, all over Serb Krajinas and in Posavina. "Now you are here in Doboj, what has been your role and assignment in Doboj? "To protect Doboj from looting and similar things, along with my men. "Describe to us what it was it like in Doboj and in Grapska since we are now here near Grapska? "I only arrived in Grapska upon invitation to regarding pulling out refugees who that set off towards our town, and that's where we assisted in the -- in transport of the refugees. But first some people slandered me on the Sarajevo television and radio, saying that at this place, which is also my neighbour's place, my machine men and I had slaughtered and torched women and children. Their inhabitants denied this yesterday and I'm denying it right now again. Neither I, nor Karagic nor Dobrivoje were here at the time of the fighting. We neither celebrated nor built fire, nor did we throw their women and children on to the bonfire, into the fire. "In the meantime, I've learned that before you came to our war affected territories, you had a temporary job abroad."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that's all we need.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bjelosevic, do you recognise the man there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's Jorgic. Nikola Jorgic, nicknamed Joja.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where is Mr. Jorgic at present?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is in Germany in prison. I think that he was arrested there in 1990-something and there was a trial and he was convicted in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was the trial about, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: War crimes committed during 1992 in Doboj; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, that's exactly the period.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted as an exhibit, please. It's tab 16A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is there an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note that this document was not on the original 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That apart, is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is my objection. The only objection I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So there would be a double application admitted 65 ter list then as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not sure. If Your Honours think that's right because it's Defence case -- so our 65 ter list is not really an issue anymore, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But if Your Honours think that it is ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P02324. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's move, please, Mr. Bjelosevic, to the question of the prison in Doboj and the prisoners. As I understood your evidence when you were asked about this -- I'll come on to that later. Could you have a look, please, at a photograph of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which is at tab 95. P1297. And it's at tab 95. Not you, Mr. Bjelosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I close this please to get it out of my way. Yes, I understand what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a recent photograph, Mr. Bjelosevic, but can you indicate to us, please, first of all, where the CSB is and then the prison. You'll be given a pen. If you could mark the CSB, once you've got your bearings, as 1 and the prison as 2.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. And is that the same position that it was in in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P02325, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may articulate my objections now. We had a number of the Prosecutor's witnesses from Doboj. These pictures are on their list. If I correctly understand, the purpose of showing the documents at this stage by the Office of the Prosecutor is to test the credible of the witness, not to further their case. That is my understanding. And based on that, all these documents which we never saw before which are having 20.000 something 65 ter numbers have been disclosed to us, and Mr. Hannis, himself, confirmed that these documents are used to test the credibility. They are not introduced for the truth of its contents, but to test the credibility of the witness. Now, the Office of the Prosecutor -- I'm not objecting to this particular document. We've been on the site visit. I think we saw that it's not contested at all. But I must say I'm a bit confused now because the previous video also could have been shown to any of the OTP witnesses. If the video was used for the test of the credibility of this witness, I don't see that he gave any wrong answer. He confirmed everything what Ms. Korner was putting to him concerning that particular issue that we were discussing. This person Nikola Jorgic. Now, I must say that I'm confused. Is this a part of the continuous of the Prosecutor's case? That is my concern, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the general prince -- I don't want to discuss it now because I've got such little time. But in this case, I think this particular photograph has been marked by other witnesses, and I don't imagine its contention. But it's important that the Trial Chamber know that this witness knows, if you see what I mean, but I really don't want to argue the principle of what the purpose of new exhibits is at this stage. We've already been through this and it's a lengthy argument, but this one, I simply don't understand what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was going to say that I didn't -- that the cross-examination of the Defence witness includes the testing of the credibility and/or reliability of the witness whether it is limited to that, and I know of no principle whereby the ordinary rules by which evidence comes in excludes evidence at this stage. Nevertheless, I shared not the present exhibit but the previous one -- I -- when I asked for objections from Defence, I, too, was surprised. I share your surprise that it would have been -- that that new bit of evidence would have come in at the instance of the Prosecution at that stage. In terms of the present photograph up on the screen, it isn't remarkable at all that -- and I go back to the practice before we had the electronic photographs, you have an album of photographs in and the witnesses, several witnesses would be shown it and indicate where their recollections were, so nothing really turns on that, it's merely a tidying-up exercise. It may be repetitious but it's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I explicitly say I'm not objecting to this particular document because it's not contested at all. What I expressed is my concern, because you see, Your Honours -- I see that the principle should be in my understanding that the Defence knows -- is made aware of the Prosecution's case, and that is the purpose of the Rule 65 and the 65 ter list. Now we are in the Defence case and the Office of the Prosecutor is introducing new evidence which have not been introduced during the Prosecutor's case nor is on the 65 ter list of the Prosecutor initially. That is my concern and that is the concern that I wanted to share with the Trial Chamber. Thank you very much. It doesn't concern the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't want to waste time arguing. We are actually rehashing the same argument over and over again. But I would like to get on -- the reasons, Your Honour, to finish this witness and we can come back to this at a later stage, if that's all right. I don't actually agree with Mr. Zecevic's assertion, and I've said that before, nor do I agree that's what Mr. Hannis said when he was dealing with this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... so your application is for the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Your application is for this photograph which we've seen before as marked by this witness to be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it may be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to understand your evidence. Is it your evidence on the prisoner, Mr. Bjelosevic, that you did not know who was in prison and had no control over what was happening --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Korner, did ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, the document was given number P2325.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is it your evidence, Mr. Bjelosevic, that you had no control over who was held in that prison or how long they were kept there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The system, if you like, however, was one that lay within your authority as head of the CSB, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What system and when? Can we be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. The whole -- not part of the Law on Internal Affairs that I took you through this morning, but the fact that there are certain prescribed norms under the law for how long prisoners may be held and the right of prisoners to know why they are being arrested?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that anybody who is arrested has to know why. A document has to be issued to that effect by the person who arrested him, but I don't know what your question is. If that is your question, then I can say that I agree that that should be the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Therefore, do you agree as the head of the CSB in Doboj, leaving aside for the moment you say you weren't there, it was your responsibility to ensure that the law was carried out, your own Serbian law was carried out in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not during that period of time. I don't agree that I was the one who could ensure that, and as you put it yourself in your previous question, that I was the one who had that under my control, I don't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I am sorry, Mr. Bjelosevic, leaving aside what you say are the special circumstances, as a matter of law, were you not responsible for the proper application of the Law on Internal Affairs as regards prisoners in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. You said no, that's fine. Just tell me, because I haven't got that much time --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me, I have to explain, please. I'm kindly asking the Trial Chamber to allow me to complete my answers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Mr. Bjelosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I took it upon myself to tell the truth and the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Give me the answer but, please, shortly, Mr. Bjelosevic. Why weren't you responsible?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the prison as an institution was under the control of the Ministry of Justice and not of the Ministry of the Interior. That's the first and most important reason. Secondly, the prison at the time and always -- it has always had its guard service that took care of the safety of the building and of the persons in the prisons. So I don't know how I was supposed to be responsible for the situation in the prison, especially bearing in mind that when once they are handed over, only the person who signed the decision on the detention can then take care of these things and nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now that's the point, sorry, not who is physically in charge of the prison and the conditions in the prison, but that the law is complied with for how long people may be kept in detention, being given the reasons for their detention, and so on. That was the responsibility of the police, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the police arrested someone, then those people who did that had the obligation to issue the decision on detention. And there always have to be some reasons to detain somebody, a procedure has to be followed, such a person has to be informed about what it is all about, I entirely agree with you about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And for that, Mr. Bjelosevic, you were the senior police officer in Doboj, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we have rehashed this topic on a number of occasions, and yet I have to repeat myself. Both according to the Law on the Interior and other regulations, the public security station is responsible for the security related matters in its area of responsibility. You had a chance to see that the Crisis Staff explicitly ordered that very same thing in its decision. It was the station, or, more precisely, the chief of the station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Let me ask you, please, to look at a document which is P1315, tab 15. Do you recognise that book?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can see is the log-book of extraction of the detainees, but I don't know what book this is. I don't recognise the handwriting, I don't know what's in it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, have you never seen a book like this before?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's just have a look and see if you recognise some of the names.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page, please, in B/C/S. I am afraid it doesn't help much in English because they didn't translate the names, just what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's deal with number 11, do you know who Jozo Mandic was?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 11? If I'm not mistaken, Jozo Mandic, if that's the person, he was the president of the HDZ in Doboj. I believe that that was his name actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How old was he?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You sure about that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but he wasn't young.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Over 70?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was over 70, but he was getting on. He was elderly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you don't know, didn't you sign a criminal report against him?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We'll come to that later. Number 12, Karlo Grgic, who was he?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karlo Grgic was a former commander of the police station in Doboj. If I'm not mistaken during this specific period of time, he was already retired.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what -- I should have asked you, first of all, what ethnicity was Jozo Mandic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since he was the president of the HDZ, I assume that he was Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Karlo Grgic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And number 13 on the list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I remind you of the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, can I just finish number 13 and then I'm done.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Number 13 on the list, who was he, do you know?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ilija Tipura. Ilija Tipura was a member of the department for foreigners. He was a member of the service.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And his nationality?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think he was a Croat, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, thank you very much. And thank you very much, Your Honours, for giving me the extra time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, well we take the adjournment for today. We are grateful to the support staff, the Court Officers, the interpreters, security staff, the stenographers for facilitating this, and we are grateful, too, for the co-operation of the accused, Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Zupljanin, in the disruption of their schedule to accommodate the extra sitting. So we reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00.
